title: Berlin and NATO — The Crystallization of the Cold War Alliance System

documents.label: A
documents.citation: President Harry S. Truman, Statement on the Berlin Airlift, July 19, 1948 — U.S. government document, available through the Harry S. Truman Presidential Library (National Archives)
documents.excerpt: We are in Berlin as a result of our agreements with our Allies after the defeat of Germany... These agreements also gave us certain rights of access to Berlin. I want the record to be absolutely clear that abandonment of our position in Berlin would mean the loss of more than a city. It would be a blow to the entire structure of resistance to Soviet expansionism.

documents.label: B
documents.citation: North Atlantic Treaty, Preamble and Article 5, April 4, 1949 — multilateral treaty, available through the Avalon Project, Yale Law School
documents.excerpt: The Parties... are determined to safeguard the freedom, common heritage and civilisation of their peoples, founded on the principles of democracy, individual liberty and the rule of law... The Parties agree that an armed attack against one or more of them in Europe or North America shall be considered an attack against them all.

documents.label: C
documents.citation: President John F. Kennedy, "Ich bin ein Berliner" speech, West Berlin, June 26, 1963 — U.S. government document, available through the John F. Kennedy Presidential Library (National Archives)
documents.excerpt: There are many people in the world who really don't understand, or say they don't, what is the great issue between the free world and the Communist world. Let them come to Berlin. Freedom is indivisible, and when one man is enslaved, all are free. The wall is the most obvious and vivid demonstration of the failures of the Communist system.
